newsitem.title: USA: Toyota Motor's Toyoda hopes for stable yen-dollar.
newsitem.headline: Toyota Motor's Toyoda hopes for stable yen-dollar.

text.p: Toyota Motor Corp Chairman Shoichiro Toyoda said Tuesday U.S. and Japanese business people should hope for a stable yen-dollar exchange rate that reflects economic fundamentals.

"As business people, we should hope for a stable exchange rate that reflects economic fundamentals," Toyoda said at a U.S.-Japan business conference in San Francisco. "We should be wary of the potential for exchange rate fluctuations due to speculation and conjecture."

Toyoda, who is also chairman of Japan's Federation of Economic Organizations (Keidanren), said U.S.-Japan relations were basically in good shape, but recent growth in Japan's trade surplus had "given rise to voices of concern."

But he said Japanese manufacturers continued to localize production in the United States and structural economic reform in Japan was opening the Japanese market. "So the trade imbalance is unlikely over the medium and long terms to expand as it has in the past. However, this positive scenario assumes a stable yen-dollar exchange rate," Toyoda said at the conference, organized by the U.S.-Japan and Japan-U.S. business councils.
Toyoda said the Japanese were reaching a consensus that their old ways of doing things were becoming unviable "amid the tides of globalization."
"People are beginning to recognize that excessive regulation imposes a heavy cost on our domestic industries. So momentum is building for reform," he said.
"Our job now is to reinforce that momentum and step up the pace of reform. I regard this year as the time to make reform happen," he said.

Toyoda said the most important challenge was to push ahead with deregulation and promote economic vitality led by domestic demand. He said the Japanese economy was recovering gradually despite concerns about the effect of a sales tax increase in April. "But we need to make sure that the recovery takes hold," he said. "We need to invigorate the Japanese economy."
He said the government had already taken steps to loosen regulations in retailing and distribution, telecommunications and financial services.

But he noted that the government's three year deregulation program ends next March. "So we need to redouble our efforts in calling on the government to continue with deregulation," said Toyoda, who spoke to the business leaders in Japanese.

He said tax reform was essential in stimulating economic vitality. The effective tax rate for large corporations in Japan was about 50 percent. "We need to bring it down at least to the U.S. level of around 40 percent," Toyoda said.

He said reforming Japan's financial system was also a pressing issue. A revised foreign exchange law that takes effect next April would permit all financial institutions to handle foreign exchange transactions. Toyoda said this would help to globalize Japan's financial services industry.
